name: MESSENGER crater
intro: MESSENGER was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury. After four years and more than 4,000 orbits, it ran out of fuel and crashed into Mercury on 30 April 2015, making a new crater about 16 meters wide. Nothing of the spacecraft is left in one piece.
whyLeft: It had used up all its fuel, so it could no longer stay up. The Sun’s pull slowly lowered its orbit until it hit the ground at about 14,000 km/h.
repurpose: Nothing is left to repair. A future Mercury orbiter could photograph its crater and learn how fresh craters change so close to the Sun.

hotspots.title: A brand-new crater
hotspots.text: Here MESSENGER hit Mercury at about 14,000 km/h on 30 April 2015, on the far side, out of sight of Earth. It blasted out a crater about 16 meters wide.

hotspots.title: The last picture
hotspots.text: MESSENGER’s final photo, taken minutes before the crash, shows a patch of Mercury’s ground only about a kilometer across, the closest look it ever had.

photo.alt: Grey close-up of Mercury’s rough surface with small craters.
photo.caption: MESSENGER’s very last picture of Mercury, taken on 30 April 2015 just before the crash.
photo.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington

hotspots.title: Running on fumes
hotspots.text: When its rocket fuel ran out, engineers found a clever trick: they used the helium gas that pushed the fuel as a tiny extra rocket, buying about a month more of science.

hotspots.title: Ice near the Sun
hotspots.text: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, yet MESSENGER found water ice hiding in deep craters near its poles, where sunlight never reaches.

hotspots.title: Its sunshade
hotspots.text: MESSENGER hid behind a sunshade of heat-proof ceramic cloth, because sunlight at Mercury can be up to 11 times stronger than on Earth. Whatever is left of it is now scattered here.

funFact: To reach Mercury without crashing into the Sun, MESSENGER flew past Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury three times before it could slip into orbit.

source.label: NASA Photojournal: Best Determination of MESSENGER's Impact Location (16 m estimate; depth assumed a fifth of the width, as for fresh craters)
